sources.title: Nawal El Moutawakel (Q239993), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-30): label 'Nawal El Moutawakel', description 'Moroccan hurdler and IOC member', born 15 April 1962, no death date, citizenship Morocco, Korean label present, P18 image 'PortraitNawalElMoutawakelJune2016.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Tom Kroeschell, 'El Moutawakel, Nawal', Iowa State University Biographical Dictionary (published 30 July 2021, CC BY 4.0), read in full: CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Her recruitment to Iowa State, her 1984 season, the inaugural Olympic women's 400 m hurdles final won in 54.61 seconds, the roles she held afterwards (Olympic committee evaluation and coordination commissions, athletics federation council, Moroccan sports posts), the women's road race she organised, and her university and state hall-of-fame inductions. University biography by the university's own historian; admiring and partly drawn from the athletics department site. Family events it mentions were not used.

Olympedia athlete biography 'Nawal El-Moutawakel' (olympedia.org/athletes/73297), read in full: eliminated in the 1983 World Championships semi-finals, the inaugural 1984 Olympic women's 400 m hurdles being 'wide open' because of the boycott by the Soviet Union and East Germany, a personal-best 54.61, first Moroccan Olympic champion and first woman from an Islamic nation to win Olympic gold, later titles, IOC roles from 1998 and the Olympic flagbearer role in 2006. Independent Olympic statistics and biography project; it supplies the competitive context the other sources omit.

World Athletics (IAAF) feature 'Nawal El Moutawakel - Pioneer and militant for Progress' (22 March 1999), read in full: her place as a role model who allowed other Arab and Muslim women to compete, her career path from the Casablanca club to Iowa State, her post-competitive coaching and administrative roles, and her statement that she needed to enter the decision-making sphere to improve women's sport. Governing-body feature from the period; admiring.

World Athletics heritage feature 'Nawal El Moutawakel: the 54 seconds that changed her life' (8 April 2021), read in full: her early career, the Iowa State scholarship, the 1984 final, and her own reflections on the opening it gave Arab and African women. Governing-body feature built on her interview quotes; celebratory, and the personal-loss passages were not used.

AFP via France 24, 'El Moutawakel, torch bearer for Muslim sportswomen' (4 March 2019), read in full: her statement that she could have stayed enjoying her 1984 glory but chose to share her experience with younger people, her remarks on women and sport in Islam, and her account of being unprepared for the press after the win. News-agency interview piece; mostly her own words.

Laureus World Sports Academy member profile 'Nawal El Moutawakel' (laureus.com), read in full: the 1984 gold, her Iowa State training, the Casablanca women's fun run she organises, her IAAF council seat (1995), IOC membership and commissions, the 2004 chair of the IOC evaluation commission for 2012, the 2012 election as an IOC Vice-President, and the Laureus Lifetime Achievement Award (2010). Award-body profile of one of its own academy members; celebratory.

'El Moutawakel, Nawal (1962-)', Gale encyclopedia entry on Encyclopedia.com, read in full: her background, titles, the Iowa State years, her Olympic gold, and a contributions section noting both that the win changed perceptions of women in sport and that many Muslims criticised her dress. Reference biography that is partly dated and gives 1998 for IOC membership where Laureus gives 1997; used as the one source that records criticism she faced.
Wikimedia Commons file page 'PortraitNawalElMoutawakelJune2016.jpg' (photograph by Citizen59, 4 June 2016, CC BY 3.0), checked for the portrait only; not used for any scoring.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_nawal_isu, src_nawal_laureus, src_nawal_encyc, src_nawal_france24 | 1990s-2019 | university biography + award-body profile + reference entry + news interview] ISU and Laureus document that she organised a large women's road race in Casablanca (the Gale entry dates its first edition to 1993) and used her position to encourage women into sport; Gale adds work on AIDS awareness and illiteracy among rural girls; in 2019 she told AFP she chose not to rest on her 1984 glory and wanted to share the experience with younger people. The actions are documented by independent institutions, but the stated motive is her own.

persistence.rationale: [src_nawal_isu, src_nawal_olympedia | 1977-1987 | university biography + Olympic statistics biography] ISU says she was a reluctant hurdler ranked 26th in the world in 1983, returned to form for Los Angeles after an ankle injury curtailed her post-collegiate season, and kept winning afterwards (four Big Eight titles, an NCAA title, two Mediterranean Games golds); Olympedia lists African, Mediterranean and Universiade titles between 1982 and 1987. These show sustained competing and a documented comeback, but the sources do not describe her own effort in detail.

adaptability.rationale: [src_nawal_isu, src_nawal_wa2021 | 1983-1989 | university biography + governing-body feature] ISU says she arrived at Iowa State in January 1983 never having seen snow and still learning English, then adjusted to become an NCAA champion in 1984; World Athletics notes the Iowa State scholarship let her refine her technique; she later moved from competition to coaching and administration. The adaptation is inferred from outcomes; no source gives her own account of the adjustment beyond the arrival anecdotes.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_nawal_isu, src_nawal_laureus, src_nawal_olympedia | 1995-2024 | university biography + award-body profile + Olympic statistics biography] She sat on the IAAF council from 1995, became an IOC member (1998 per Olympedia, 1997 per Laureus), chaired the IOC evaluation commission for the 2012 Games (ISU describes her as the first woman to chair it), became an IOC Vice-President in 2012 and held executive-board seats. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 68 / 0.55 to 64 / 0.50 because the evidence is a list of appointments from admiring institutions with no behavioural account of how she led. Ministerial posts are political context and unscored.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_nawal_wa1999, src_nawal_isu | 1989-1999 | governing-body feature + university biography] The 1999 World Athletics feature says she understood very early that she needed to enter the decision-making sphere to improve women's sport, and both sources record her moving from coaching at grass-roots level to national athletics posts and federation bodies after returning to Morocco in 1989-1990. This shows a pattern of taking on roles, but the stated reasoning comes from one contemporary feature that quotes her.

portrait.source: Wikimedia Commons, 'PortraitNawalElMoutawakelJune2016.jpg', photograph by the Commons user Citizen59, taken 4 June 2016 in Tunis and described on the file page as showing Nawal El Moutawakel. The file page carries camera metadata (Nikon D300 with a 70-300 mm lens, serial number recorded, original time stamp 4 June 2016), structured data naming Citizen59 as photographer with 'original creation by uploader', and a first-party CC BY 3.0 statement; it was uploaded 8 July 2016 and edited once for contrast by the same user. Original 1203 x 1385 pixels, downscaled to 1042 x 1200 with no cropping and no upscaling. Caveat: the sitter and event are identified only by the uploader's description, although the image has been the lead image of the subject on many Wikipedia editions.
